17080:
The adjective veterinary means relating to the medical care, health, and treatment of animals. Whenever you see this word, it is simply telling you: "this thing belongs to, or is connected with, the world of animal medicine."

Think of it this way: just as the word medical describes things related to human healthcare (a medical doctor, a medical clinic, medical advice), the word veterinary describes things related to animal healthcare. It is the animal-world equivalent of medical.

Veterinary applies to all animals — not just pets. This includes:

  • Companion animals like dogs, cats, and rabbits.
  • Farm and livestock animals like cows, pigs, sheep, and horses.
  • Wild animals like lions, eagles, or elephants (in zoos or wildlife rescue).
  • Exotic animals like reptiles, birds, and fish.

So it is not limited to your neighbor's pet dog. A zoo doctor treating a giraffe, a scientist studying disease in fish, and a nurse helping a cow give birth are all operating in the veterinary world.

As an adjective, veterinary is always placed in front of a noun to describe it. Here are the most common things it describes:

Veterinary medicine — the entire branch of science and practice dedicated to keeping animals healthy, diagnosing their illnesses, and treating them. It is the animal equivalent of human medicine.

Veterinary surgeon / veterinary doctor — the professional who is trained and qualified to treat animals. In everyday speech, people usually just call this person a vet. The full formal title is veterinary surgeon.

Veterinary clinic / veterinary hospital — the physical place where animals go to be examined and treated. Just like humans go to a hospital or clinic, sick or injured animals go to a veterinary clinic.

Veterinary care — the overall attention, treatment, and services provided to keep an animal healthy. "The injured bird received excellent veterinary care."

Veterinary science — the academic and scientific study of animal health, diseases, anatomy, and medicine.

Veterinary nurse / veterinary technician — a trained support professional who assists the veterinary surgeon, much like a nurse assists a human doctor.

Veterinary treatment — the specific procedures, medicines, or therapies given to an animal for a health problem.

Veterinary advice — guidance or recommendations given by a qualified animal-health professional about an animal's health.

Veterinary examination — a physical check-up of an animal done by a vet.

Veterinary practice — this can mean two things: (1) the act of practicing veterinary medicine as a profession, or (2) the business/office where a vet works.

• "She decided to study veterinary medicine because she loves animals."
  • "The dog was taken to a veterinary clinic after swallowing something dangerous."
  • "The farmer called for veterinary assistance when his horses fell ill."
  • "Veterinary science has advanced so much that animals can now have surgery similar to what humans receive."
  • "Always seek veterinary advice before giving your pet any medicine."
The Key Idea to Always Remember

If you ever see the word veterinary and feel unsure, just replace it in your mind with the phrase "to do with animal medicine" — and the sentence will make complete sense. It is always pointing you toward the world of animal health. That is its one, clear, consistent job as an adjective.
17081:
A veto is an official power or act of saying "No — this will not happen" in a way that is strong enough to stop or block a decision, even if everyone else agrees to it.

The key thing to understand right away is that a veto is not just a regular "no." When you or I say no to something, it can be overruled or ignored. But a veto is a special, authorised "no" — one that carries enough legal or official weight to actually stop something from going forward.

Think of it like a giant red STOP button that only certain people are allowed to press — and when they press it, the machine stops, no matter what.

Imagine a group of five friends voting on where to eat dinner. Four of them vote for pizza. But the fifth friend has a special rule that says his "no" can cancel the whole decision. So even though four people wanted pizza, that one person's "no" shuts it down entirely. That power — that official, decision-killing "no" — is a veto.

In more serious, real-world terms: a veto is the right or the act of blocking something that has been proposed or even already agreed upon by others.
The Two Faces of the Word

As a noun, "veto" can refer to two slightly different things, and it's important to know both.

First, it refers to the power or right itself — the authority someone holds to block decisions. For example: "The president has a veto over new laws." Here, "veto" means the official power that exists, whether or not it's been used yet.

Second, it refers to the act of using that power — the actual blocking of a specific decision. For example: "The president issued a veto." Here, "veto" means the concrete action of rejecting something.

So the word can describe the weapon itself, or the act of firing that weapon. Both uses are completely standard and correct.

In Government (The Most Famous Use)

The most well-known use of the veto is in politics. In many countries, a president or a monarch is given the power to reject a law that has been passed by the parliament or legislature. The lawmakers vote, they agree, they pass the bill — but then the head of state can say "no" and block it from becoming law. That act of rejection is called a veto.

In the United States, for instance, after the Congress passes a bill, the President can veto it, sending it back without signing it into law.

Now, here's an important nuance: a veto doesn't always mean "never." In many systems, a veto can be overridden — meaning if enough people in the group push back strongly enough (for example, a two-thirds majority), they can force the decision through anyway, overruling the veto. So a veto is powerful, but it is not always the final word. Whether it can be overridden or not depends entirely on the rules of the system in question.

At the United Nations

One of the most powerful vetoes in the world belongs to the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council — the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom, and France. If any one of these five countries casts a veto, a resolution (an official international decision) is blocked entirely, even if all the other member countries supported it. This veto cannot be overridden. It is absolute. This makes it a far stronger form of veto than most.

In Companies and Organisations

Vetoes also exist in the business world. A major shareholder, a board member, or a founding partner might be given veto power over certain company decisions. This means that even if the rest of the board agrees on something, that one person can stop it from happening.

In Everyday Life

The word "veto" is also used informally in everyday situations, outside of politics or law. A parent might say, "I have veto power over where we go on holiday," meaning they have the final say to reject any option they don't like. In this casual usage, the word keeps its core meaning — a powerful, decision-stopping "no" — but it's used loosely, without any official or legal weight behind it.
The Essential Qualities of a Veto

To truly understand what makes something a veto (and not just a regular objection), keep these three qualities in mind.

It must be authorised — the person using it must have been given the right to do so by a system, a set of rules, or a law. A random person cannot simply declare a veto.

It must be powerful enough to stop something — a veto has practical consequences. It doesn't just express disagreement; it actually blocks or cancels the decision.

It is typically used by one person or a small group — the whole point of a veto is that one voice can override many. If everyone had veto power equally, it wouldn't be special.
A Few Common Phrases You'll Encounter

"Veto power" — this refers to the right or authority to veto. Someone who has veto power can choose to use it or not use it. Simply having the power doesn't mean it has been used yet.

"To exercise a veto" — this means to actually use the veto, to carry out the act of blocking something. It's a slightly formal way of saying "to veto something."

"The veto was overridden" — this means the veto was challenged and defeated. The decision that was blocked went through anyway because enough people pushed back against the veto.

"A pocket veto" — this is a specific political term used in the United States. Normally, if a president does nothing with a bill — neither signs it nor vetoes it — it can become law on its own after a set number of days. But if Congress is not in session during those days, the president's inaction effectively kills the bill. This silent, do-nothing blocking is called a pocket veto, because the president essentially "pockets" the bill and does nothing. It's a veto achieved through silence rather than an active rejection.

The word veto captures a simple but profound idea: that in many systems — governments, organisations, families — not all voices carry equal weight when it comes to blocking decisions. A veto is the formalised, authorised power to say "This stops here," and to actually make it stop.

It is a tool of control, of balance, and sometimes of protection — used to prevent decisions that one party finds unacceptable, even when they are outnumbered. Whether it's a world leader rejecting a law, a nation blocking an international resolution, or a parent saying no to a holiday destination, the spirit of the word is always the same: one empowered "no" that can stop the many.
17082:
When you veto something, you officially and authoritatively reject or block a decision, plan, or law — stopping it from happening — even if other people have already agreed to it or voted for it.

The single most important thing to understand is this: a veto is not just a "no" from anyone. It is a powerful, formal "no" that actually kills or stops something. And only certain people, in certain roles, have the power to use it.

Imagine a group of people vote on a decision. The majority agrees. Everything seems settled. But then one specific person — someone with special authority — steps in and says, "I reject this. It will not go forward." That act of blocking it? That is a veto.

So to veto something is to:

  • Refuse to approve it, and
  • Use your authority to prevent it from taking effect.

Both parts matter. A regular person can refuse to approve something, but their refusal doesn't necessarily stop it. When someone vetoes it, their refusal does stop it — because they hold the power to do so.

In government (the most common context):

In many countries, a president or a monarch can veto a bill (a proposed law) that has been passed by the legislature (the parliament or congress). This means even though the lawmakers voted "yes," the president can step in and say "no," and the bill does not become a law.

For example: "The president vetoed the bill, so it never became a law."

In international bodies:

In the United Nations Security Council, five powerful countries (the US, UK, France, Russia, and China) each have the right to veto any major resolution. If even one of them vetoes it, the resolution is blocked — no matter how many other countries supported it.

For example: "Russia vetoed the resolution, so the Security Council could not take action."

In everyday informal use:

People also use "veto" more loosely in everyday life to mean firmly shooting down someone's idea — often humorously.

For example: "I suggested we go camping, but my wife vetoed it immediately."
Or: "The kids wanted pizza every night, but Dad vetoed that plan."

Here, the word still carries the same flavour — one person using their authority (as a spouse, a parent, a boss) to block what others wanted.
What a Veto Does NOT Mean

This is subtle but important:

  • Vetoing something does not always mean it is gone forever. In many systems, a veto can be overridden — meaning if enough people push back strongly enough (for example, a two-thirds majority in the US Congress), they can reverse the veto and make the decision stand anyway.
  • Vetoing something is not the same as simply disagreeing. You can disagree with something all you want, but you can only veto it if you have been given the formal authority to do so.
  • A veto is not a punishment. It is a mechanism — a built-in check — that gives certain people the power to block decisions they find unacceptable.

"Veto" carries a sense of finality and authority. When someone vetoes something, it lands with weight. It is decisive. It shuts a door. This is why the word is also used dramatically in casual conversation — when you veto your friend's bad idea for a road trip, you're borrowing that sense of firm, no-nonsense authority.
To veto something is to officially use your authority to reject and block it, preventing it from moving forward — regardless of who else agreed to it.
17083:
To vex someone means to cause them to feel annoyed, frustrated, or troubled — but with a very specific flavour worth understanding carefully.

It is not the sharp, explosive feeling of sudden rage. It is more of a persistent, nagging irritation — the kind that settles in and lingers. Think of vex as a slow simmer rather than a sudden boil.

Here's a simple picture: if someone bumps into you once by accident, you might feel a flash of irritation. That's not vex. But if the same person keeps interrupting you every time you speak, ignores your feelings, and repeats the behaviour again and again — that deep, building frustration you carry? That is what it means to be vexed.

Three things can vex a person:

A person can vex someone else. "His constant complaining vexed everyone at the table."

A situation can vex someone. "The hours-long traffic jam vexed the commuters greatly."

A problem or puzzle can vex someone. "The unsolved mystery vexed the detective for years." In this sense, vex means to baffle or perplex — to trouble the mind because something cannot be figured out. This use is slightly older and more formal, but you will encounter it in literature and careful writing.

Vex sits at a moderate level on the emotional scale. It is stronger than "slightly bother" but not as severe as "enrage." A rough scale to picture it:

mildly bother → irritate → vex → distress → infuriate

So if someone is vexed, they are genuinely bothered — not just mildly inconvenienced, but also not in a state of rage. They are somewhere in that uncomfortable middle ground of nagging frustration.

"The noise from the neighbours vexed him every morning." (A situation vexing a person)

"Her careless attitude vexed her supervisor." (A person's behaviour vexing another)

"The riddle had vexed scholars for centuries." (A problem baffling/troubling people)

"I was vexed to learn that my advice had been ignored." (Feeling annoyed about something)

Notice that vex is often paired with the person being affected as the subject when using the passive form: "I was vexed" rather than "something vexed me" — though both are correct.
Related Word Forms You Must Know

Vexed (adjective): This describes the state of feeling annoyed or troubled. "She wore a vexed expression." "He was vexed by the delay."

Vexing (adjective): This describes the thing or situation that is causing the annoyance. "It was a truly vexing problem." "His behaviour was vexing to everyone around him."

Vexation (noun): The feeling itself — the state of being vexed. "She struggled to hide her vexation." "It was a source of great vexation to him."

This is important. When someone calls something "a vexed question" or "a vexed issue," it does not mean the question is annoyed. It means the question or topic is one that has troubled people's minds for a very long time — it is deeply controversial, debated, and unresolved.

"The question of how to achieve lasting peace in the region remains a deeply vexed one."

This usage flows naturally from the original meaning: the issue has "troubled" so many minds, for so long, that it has become a vexed matter. You will see this phrase often in journalism, academic writing, and formal speech.

"Vex" has a slightly formal or literary flavour in standard English. In everyday casual conversation, people tend to say "annoyed," "frustrated," or "bothered" instead. You are more likely to read vex in a novel, an essay, or careful writing than to hear it in casual speech.

However, there is an important exception: in Caribbean English — spoken in Jamaica, Trinidad, Barbados, and other islands — "vex" is a completely everyday, informal word. There, it simply and directly means angry or upset. "She vex with me bad" means "she is very angry with me." This is a rich, living use of the word that you may encounter in Caribbean literature, music, and conversation.

To vex is to cause someone a persistent, nagging sense of annoyance, frustration, or distress — not a sudden explosion of anger, but a deep, simmering irritation that troubles them and stays with them.
17084:
Vexation means a feeling of irritation, frustration, and inner disturbance — usually caused by something that is persistently annoying, difficult to fix, or beyond your control.

Think of it as that specific feeling you get when something keeps going wrong, or keeps bothering you, and you feel helpless about it. It is not just a quick flash of anger. It lingers. It nags at you.
The Two Faces of the Word

"Vexation" carries two closely related meanings, and understanding both will give you full command of the word.

Meaning 1 — The feeling itself:
Vexation is the inner state of being annoyed, troubled, or frustrated. It is what you feel when something vexes you.

"He sat in traffic for two hours, and the vexation showed clearly on his face."

Here, vexation is the emotion — the irritated, wound-up feeling inside him.

Meaning 2 — The thing that causes the feeling:
A vexation can also be the source of the trouble — the actual person, thing, situation, or problem that is causing someone to feel irritated and bothered.

"The slow internet connection was a constant vexation to her."

Here, the slow internet is itself called "a vexation" — it is the thing doing the vexing.

Both meanings are correct and widely used. Context will always make it clear which one is meant.
What the Feeling of Vexation Actually Feels Like

This is important, because understanding the texture of an emotion-word is what lets you use it naturally.

Vexation is not pure, explosive anger. It is more like a slow-burning, nagging irritation mixed with a sense of helplessness. It often carries these elements:

  • A feeling that something is unfair, unreasonable, or unnecessarily difficult
  • A sense that the problem is not easily solved — or keeps repeating
  • A mild but persistent inner tension, like a knot that will not come undone
  • Sometimes, a hint of worry or distress alongside the irritation

Imagine someone who keeps making small mistakes at work despite being told. You are not furious — but you are not merely mildly annoyed either. There is a growing, festering frustration. That is vexation.

Or imagine you are trying to explain something to someone, and they simply do not understand it no matter how many times you try. The feeling that builds up inside you — part frustration, part helplessness, part low-level agitation — is vexation.

Emotions exist on a spectrum. Knowing where vexation sits helps you use it with precision.

Mild irritation → Annoyance → Vexation → Anger → Fury → Rage

Vexation is above casual annoyance but below outright anger. It is a meaningful, noticeable emotional disturbance — not trivial, but not explosive either. It is the word for when something has gotten under your skin in a way that simple "annoyance" does not fully capture.
How Vexation Differs From Similar Words

These words are close neighbours, but they are not the same:

Annoyance is lighter and more surface-level. You can be annoyed for a second and move on. Vexation runs deeper and tends to persist.

Frustration is specifically about being blocked from achieving a goal — like trying to open a jar and failing. Vexation is broader. It includes frustration but also covers worry, disturbance, and nagging irritation that is not necessarily goal-related.

Irritation is close to vexation, but it often refers to a quick, immediate reaction to a stimulus — like a buzzing fly. Vexation implies more weight, more duration, and more inner churning.

Agitation is more physical and restless — a more anxious, energetic disturbance. Vexation is more internal and brooding.

In short, vexation is what happens when irritation and frustration settle in and make themselves at home.
When and Where Is This Word Used?

Vexation is a slightly formal or literary word. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Written English (books, articles, essays)
  • Formal or educated speech
  • Older literature and classic novels

In casual, everyday speech, people more commonly say "frustration" or "annoyance." But vexation is absolutely a living, modern word — and using it correctly marks you as someone with a refined command of English.

Here are natural ways vexation appears in real sentences:

  • "Much to my vexation..." — a very common phrase meaning "to my great frustration and annoyance..."

    "Much to my vexation, the form had to be filled out again from scratch."

  • "A source of vexation" — something that repeatedly causes the feeling

    "The broken gate was a daily source of vexation for the whole neighbourhood."

  • "To someone's great vexation"

    "To his great vexation, the hotel had given away his reserved room."

  • "The vexations of..." (plural) — the many small, irritating troubles of something

    "The vexations of modern travel — delays, lost luggage, cancellations — can exhaust even the most patient person."

  • "Feel / express / hide vexation"

    "She tried to hide her vexation, but her clipped tone gave her away."

When used in the plural — vexations — it refers to multiple sources of irritation or repeated incidents of being troubled.

"Life is full of small vexations, but it is also full of small joys."

This plural form is especially common when talking about the accumulated minor irritants of everyday life.
Putting It All Together — Rich Example Sentences

Read these carefully. Each one shows a slightly different shade of the word:

  1. "The train was delayed again, and she felt a fresh wave of vexation wash over her."

— The pure feeling; it is internal.

  1. "The noisy neighbours were a constant vexation — they showed no consideration for anyone else."

— The neighbours themselves are "a vexation," meaning the cause of irritation.

  1. "Much to his vexation, the document he had spent hours writing was accidentally deleted."

— Classic phrase; notice the helplessness and frustration combined.

  1. "She sighed deeply, trying to contain her vexation before speaking calmly."

— Vexation as something you feel rising inside you, something you must manage.

  1. "The vexations of parenthood are real, but so are its rewards."

— Plural; the many small, difficult, nagging challenges.

  1. "His vexation was understandable — the same error had been made three times despite clear instructions."

— Vexation that is justified, involving repetition, helplessness, and disturbance.
One Final, Memorable Way to Think About It

If someone asked you to picture vexation, picture this:

You are trying to pour a glass of water. The tap works fine — until it doesn't. You fix it. It breaks again. You fix it again. It breaks a third time. You are not slamming doors in rage. But there is a tight, growing, "I cannot believe this is happening again" feeling building inside you.

That is vexation. The irritation that comes not from one sharp blow, but from persistent, nagging trouble that tests your patience and sense of control.
17085:
Vexatious means causing persistent annoyance, frustration, or distress — usually in a way that feels unnecessary, unreasonable, or hard to escape. If something is vexatious, it doesn't just bother you once and go away. It keeps nagging at you, wearing you down, or making things harder than they need to be.

Think of it this way: a single mosquito bite is annoying. But a cloud of mosquitoes that follows you everywhere, ruining your entire evening no matter what you do? That's vexatious.
The Feeling It Captures

What separates "vexatious" from plain old "annoying" is a subtle but important layer: vexatious things tend to feel unjustified or needlessly created. The frustration they cause is not just uncomfortable — it feels pointless or unfair, like it shouldn't even exist in the first place.

For example:

  • A difficult task that makes sense to do is hard, but not vexatious.
  • A pile of redundant paperwork that solves no real problem and just wastes your time? That is vexatious.

There's also often a sense of helplessness baked in. A vexatious situation is one you can't easily fix or walk away from, which is part of what makes it so frustrating.
Who or What Can Be Vexatious?

The word can describe a wide range of things:

  • Situations: bureaucratic delays, unclear rules, endless obstacles
  • Behavior: someone who nitpicks, interrupts, or complains repeatedly without good reason
  • Problems: issues that keep resurfacing and resisting solutions
  • People: someone whose actions persistently and unreasonably trouble others

Note that when used to describe a person, it usually refers to their behavior or manner, not their character as a whole. You'd more naturally say "his behavior is vexatious" than "he is a vexatious person," though both are grammatically fine.
How Strong Is It? (The Intensity Scale)

Vexatious sits comfortably in the middle-to-upper range of annoyance — stronger than "mildly irritating" but not as explosive as "infuriating" or "enraging."

A rough scale for comparison:
Mildly annoying → Irritating → Vexatious → Infuriating → Enraging

It implies real, meaningful frustration — not something you'd brush off — but it doesn't necessarily make you lose your temper. It's more the kind of frustration that builds slowly and wears you down over time.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Similar WordKey Difference

Annoying is casual and everyday. You call a song stuck in your head "annoying." You would rarely call it vexatious — that would sound overly dramatic for something so minor.

Irritating is similar in everyday strength, but vexatious is more formal and implies more persistence and a greater sense of injustice.

Troublesome focuses on the trouble or difficulty something causes. Vexatious emphasizes the emotional frustration more directly.

Irksome is probably the closest synonym — also formal, also meaning persistently annoying — but vexatious is slightly stronger and more commonly used in serious or legal writing.

Infuriating is much stronger. Vexatious doesn't imply outright anger, just deep, persistent frustration.
The Legal Meaning (A Specific, Important Use)

In the world of law, vexatious has a precise and well-established meaning that you should know.

A vexatious lawsuit (or vexatious claim, or vexatious litigation) is a legal case that has no genuine legal merit and is filed purely to harass, intimidate, or exhaust the other party — not to seek real justice. The person filing it knows, or should know, that the case has no real basis. Their goal is simply to cause trouble, waste the opponent's time and money, or pressure them into settling.

Courts take this seriously. A judge can declare someone a "vexatious litigant" — an official legal label for a person who has a pattern of filing baseless lawsuits just to torment others. Once labeled this way, that person may be banned from filing new lawsuits without getting special permission from the court first.

In legal language, you'll also see:

  • Vexatious proceedings
  • Vexatious complaints
  • Vexatious claim

All carry the same idea: deliberately causing hardship through a legal process, without legitimate justification.
Example Sentences

Here are examples showing both the general and legal uses in context:

General use:

  • "The constant back-and-forth emails from the committee were vexatious — nothing ever got decided."
  • "She found his vexatious habit of restarting arguments she thought were settled deeply exhausting."
  • "The new visa requirements were vexatious to travelers who had to submit the same documents three times."
  • "It was a vexatious situation: every solution they tried only created two new problems."

Legal use:

  • "The judge dismissed the case as vexatious, noting it was clearly designed to drain the defendant's resources."
  • "After filing seventeen baseless lawsuits, he was declared a vexatious litigant and barred from further filings."
  • "The company's lawyers argued that the complaint was vexatious and had no legal foundation."
Related Word Forms

The word "vexatious" belongs to a small family of related words. Knowing them strengthens your understanding:

Vex (verb) — to annoy or frustrate someone. "His vague answers vexed her deeply."

Vexed (adjective) — This has two distinct uses:

  1. Feeling annoyed or troubled. "She looked vexed after the long argument."
  2. Describing a topic that is complicated, controversial, and hard to resolve — "a vexed question," meaning one that has been debated endlessly without a clear answer.

Vexation (noun) — the state of feeling frustrated/annoyed; or the thing that causes that feeling. "He sighed in vexation." / "The traffic was a constant vexation."

Vexatiously (adverb) — in a vexatious manner. "He vexatiously dragged the meeting on for hours with pointless objections."

Vexatiousness (noun) — the quality of being vexatious. "The vexatiousness of the process drove everyone away." (Less common; "vexation" is usually preferred.)
Common Phrases and Combinations (Collocations)

Certain words pair naturally with "vexatious." Here are the most common combinations you'll encounter:

  • Vexatious litigation / litigant / lawsuit / claim / proceedings — all legal uses
  • Vexatious behavior / conduct — describing how someone acts
  • Vexatious delays / obstacles / regulations — describing frustrating systemic problems
  • Vexatious complaints — complaints filed repeatedly without genuine cause
  • Vexatious question — a problem or issue that is persistently difficult or unresolved
When and Where to Use This Word

Vexatious is a formal word. You won't typically hear it in casual conversation between friends — it lives most naturally in:

  • Legal documents and court judgments
  • Formal writing and journalism
  • Literature and serious essays
  • Professional or official complaints

If you use it in casual speech, it will come across as deliberately elevated — which can sometimes be used for effect (slightly humorous exaggeration) or may simply sound out of place. In writing, especially formal writing, it is perfectly at home and sounds precise and intelligent.
One-Line Summary
Vexatious means persistently and unreasonably annoying or frustrating — and in law, it specifically describes legal actions filed with no genuine merit, purely to harass or burden another person.
17086: Vexed has two distinct meanings depending on how it is used. Both are important, and knowing both will make you fully fluent with this word.
Meaning 1 — Feeling annoyed, troubled, or frustrated

When a person is described as vexed, they are feeling a kind of irritated annoyance — the sort of feeling you get when something keeps bothering you, going wrong, or refusing to be resolved.

It is not rage or fury. It is not a brief flash of irritation either. It sits somewhere in between: a persistent, nagging frustration — the kind that builds when you are dealing with something troublesome that won't go away, or when someone keeps doing something that gets on your nerves.

Think of it this way: if someone keeps interrupting you while you are trying to work, and you have asked them to stop more than once, the feeling you end up with — that tight, fed-up, bothered feeling — is exactly what vexed describes.

Examples:

  • She was vexed by the constant noise from the street outside.
  • He grew increasingly vexed when his computer crashed for the third time.
  • The teacher was vexed that no one had done the assignment.

Notice that in all these cases, the feeling has a cause, and that cause tends to be something the person finds difficult, unfair, or hard to control. This is key — vexed almost always implies something is making you feel this way, not just a mood you woke up with.

How strong is the emotion?
On a scale of emotional intensity, vexed is moderately strong — clearly more than mildly annoyed, but not as overwhelming as furious or enraged. It carries a sense of weariness too, like you have been patient but are running low on patience.
Meaning 2 — A vexed question / vexed issue / vexed problem

This is a completely different use of the word, but just as common and important. When vexed is used to describe a topic, question, or issue (not a person), it means the topic is difficult, deeply complicated, and long-debated — something that has been argued about for a long time without anyone arriving at a clear or agreed-upon answer.

The logic connecting this to Meaning 1 is intuitive: a vexed question is one that vexes (troubles, frustrates) the people who try to answer it.

Examples:

  • Immigration has long been a vexed issue in many democracies.
  • The vexed question of how to fairly distribute wealth has no simple answer.
  • Scientists continue to debate the vexed problem of consciousness.

A "vexed question" is not just a hard question — it is specifically one that causes disagreement, resists easy answers, and tends to generate ongoing debate. When you hear this phrase, it signals: this is a thorny, contested, complicated matter — tread carefully.

Vexed is a slightly formal word. You are more likely to encounter it in books, essays, journalism, formal speeches, or careful writing than in casual everyday speech. In ordinary conversation, people might instead say annoyed, frustrated, or bothered — but vexed is chosen when the writer or speaker wants to convey something a bit more precise or slightly literary in tone.

It is also notably common in British English, though it is by no means absent from American English.
How it differs from similar words

• Annoyed is the closest everyday equivalent for Meaning 1, but vexed implies a deeper, more sustained frustration — and a stronger sense that something is causing the feeling.
  • Frustrated is similar but leans more toward the feeling of being blocked or unable to succeed. Vexed is more about being troubled and bothered.
  • Irritated is milder — a small, quick reaction. Vexed is heavier and more lasting.

UseWhat it means
Describing a personFeeling persistently annoyed, troubled, and frustrated by something
Describing an issue/questionDeeply complicated, long-debated, and difficult to resolve

The single word that sits at the heart of vexed in both its uses is trouble — either you are troubled (Meaning 1), or the subject itself is troubling to everyone who touches it (Meaning 2).
17087:
Vexing describes something that causes a feeling of persistent annoyance, frustration, or worry — especially when that thing is difficult to deal with, solve, or make sense of. If something is vexing, it bothers you, gets under your skin, and keeps nagging at you.

Think of it this way: if something merely annoys you once and you move on, that's not really vexing. But if something keeps troubling you, sits in the back of your mind, and makes you feel stuck or helpless — that is vexing.

When something is vexing, the person experiencing it feels a mix of:

  • Frustration — it's not going the way it should.
  • Irritation — it keeps bothering them.
  • Sometimes helplessness — they can't easily fix or escape it.

It is not explosive anger. It is more like a persistent itch you cannot scratch, or a knot you cannot untie. It wears on you steadily.

"Vexing" sits in the middle range of negative feelings. Here's a simple scale to place it:

Slightly annoying → Vexing → Deeply frustrating → Infuriating → Enraging

It is stronger than a minor inconvenience, but it does not mean something makes you lose your temper. It is that stubborn, lingering kind of trouble.
What Kinds of Things Are Called "Vexing"?

This is a versatile word. It is used to describe three main things:

1. Problems or questions that are hard to solve
This is its most common and most powerful use. When a problem is complex, confusing, or has no easy answer, people call it vexing. It suggests the problem has been wrestled with, perhaps for a long time, and continues to resist resolution.

"Climate change remains one of the most vexing challenges of our time."
"The detective faced a vexing mystery with no clear clues."
"The final math question on the exam was particularly vexing."

2. Situations that are persistently irritating
A situation can be vexing when it keeps going wrong, keeps creating trouble, or just won't improve no matter what you do.

"The constant delays on her daily commute were vexing."
"It was vexing to wait an hour only to be told the office was closed."

3. People or behaviors that consistently irritate
A person's habit or behavior can be described as vexing when it repeatedly gets on your nerves.

"His habit of interrupting everyone during meetings was vexing to the whole team."
"She found his vague, non-committal answers vexing."
A Closer Look at the "Difficult to Solve" Sense

This deserves extra attention because it is very important. "Vexing" is frequently used in formal, academic, political, and professional writing to describe problems that are genuinely hard — not just personally annoying but objectively complex and resistant to simple solutions.

When someone calls a political issue, a scientific question, or a social challenge "vexing," they are signalling: "This is not simple. Smart people have tried and struggled with this. It does not have a clean answer."

So the word carries a hint of intellectual respect for the difficulty of the problem, not just personal irritation.

"Poverty is a vexing issue because its causes are deeply intertwined."
"The question of how to balance freedom and security is a vexing one for democracies."

Annoying — more casual and mild. An annoying sound. A vexing problem is deeper than just annoying.

Frustrating — very close in meaning. The difference is subtle: frustrating tends to focus on the feeling of being blocked from a goal. Vexing adds the extra layer of persistent irritation and complexity. All vexing things are frustrating, but not all frustrating things are vexing.

Troubling — focuses more on worry or concern, less on irritation. Vexing has more of an edge of active frustration to it.

Perplexing — means confusing or puzzling. Something perplexing baffles you. Something vexing bothers and frustrates you. They can overlap — a vexing problem is often also perplexing — but perplexing is purely about confusion, while vexing is about the frustration that comes with it.
Tone and Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Vexing" sits slightly above everyday casual speech. You won't hear it in very informal conversations as often as "annoying," but it is not overly formal either. It appears comfortably in:

  • Journalism and news writing
  • Academic and professional writing
  • Literature and novels
  • Thoughtful everyday conversation when someone wants to express a nuanced kind of frustration

If you use it in conversation, it sounds educated and precise. It shows you are not just saying something is "annoying" — you are saying it is the kind of thing that persists, resists solutions, and genuinely wears on the mind.

If you want a simple sentence to lock the meaning in your memory:

"Vexing" = persistently annoying and difficult to deal with.

Or picture this: you are trying to solve a puzzle and a piece just won't fit no matter how you turn it, and you've been at it for twenty minutes. That puzzle piece is vexing.

"Vexing" is an adjective meaning causing persistent frustration and irritation, especially when something is difficult to resolve or understand. It can describe hard problems, difficult situations, or irritating behaviors. It is stronger than "slightly annoying" but does not imply rage. Its most powerful and frequent use is to describe complex problems — social, political, scientific, personal — that resist easy solutions. It carries a tone that is moderately formal and precise, making it a strong, expressive word for communicating sophisticated frustration.

Viable means capable of working, surviving, or succeeding in the real world — not just in theory, but in actual practice.

The single most important idea locked inside this word is real-world practicality. When you say something is viable, you are saying it has a genuine, realistic chance of functioning, living, or being achieved. It's not a dream. It's not wishful thinking. It's something that can actually hold up and work.

This is the most important thing to understand, and many learners miss it.

Something can be possible without being viable. "Possible" simply means it could happen — there's no absolute barrier stopping it. "Viable" is a stronger, more demanding word. It means it not only can happen, but it has a solid, realistic foundation to actually work and sustain itself.

Think of it this way. It is technically possible to open a restaurant in the middle of a remote desert. There's no law against it. But it is not viable — there are no customers, no supply chains, no water. It cannot realistically survive. The moment you ask "Can this actually work and hold together in the real world?", you are asking whether something is viable.

So viable = genuinely capable of working or surviving, in a practical, sustainable way.
The Two Big Worlds Where "Viable" Is Used

1. The World of Ideas, Plans, and Options

This is the most common everyday use. Here, "viable" means a plan, solution, strategy, or option is realistic and workable — it can genuinely be carried out and lead to success.

  • "We need a viable plan before we start." — We need a plan that can actually work, not just one that sounds nice.
  • "There are only two viable options left." — Out of all the choices, only two have a real chance of working.
  • "Is this a viable solution to the problem?" — Can this actually solve the problem in practice?

When someone says a plan "isn't viable," they mean it looks good on the surface but would fall apart in reality — maybe it costs too much, takes too long, requires resources that don't exist, or simply won't produce the desired result.

2. The World of Living Things (Biology and Medicine)

In science and medicine, "viable" means a living organism or cell is capable of surviving and functioning on its own.

  • A viable fetus is one that has developed enough to survive outside the mother's womb, typically with or without medical support. A fetus that cannot survive outside is called "not viable."
  • A viable seed is one that is alive and capable of germinating (sprouting and growing into a plant). A dead seed that will never sprout is non-viable.
  • Viable cells in a lab are living cells that are functioning normally. Dead or damaged cells that cannot function are non-viable.

In all these biological cases, the core question is the same: Can this living thing survive and function on its own?

In business and economics, a viable business or venture is one that can generate enough income or value to survive and sustain itself financially over time. A business idea that would immediately collapse under its own costs is not viable, no matter how creative it is.

  • "The startup is not yet commercially viable." — It isn't generating enough revenue to survive on its own yet.
  • "We need to make the project economically viable." — We need to make it financially sustainable and worthwhile.

In politics, a viable candidate is one who has a realistic chance of winning — enough support, resources, and public backing to be a genuine contender, not just a symbolic participant.

Here are the most frequent combinations you'll see "viable" used in:

  • viable option / viable alternative — a realistic choice that could actually work
  • viable solution — an answer to a problem that can genuinely be implemented
  • viable plan / viable strategy — a course of action with a real chance of success
  • commercially viable — capable of making money and surviving in the marketplace
  • economically viable — financially sustainable and worthwhile
  • financially viable — having enough money/funding to survive
  • viable candidate — a political contender with a genuine chance of winning
  • viable fetus / viable pregnancy — a pregnancy far enough along that the baby could survive
  • viable business — a business that can sustain itself over time

The opposite of viable is expressed as not viable, unviable, or non-viable (the last one is mostly used in science and medicine).

These words mean something cannot realistically work, survive, or succeed. A plan called "not viable" is one that sounds promising but would fail in practice. A "non-viable" embryo in a medical context is one that cannot develop and survive.

"Viable" is not the highest praise you can give something. It sits in the middle of the scale — it means something can work and survive, but it doesn't necessarily mean it's the best or the most efficient option. Think of it as a baseline of approval:

  • Below viable → it won't work, it will fail or die
  • Viable → it can genuinely work and survive
  • Above viable → it's not just workable, it's excellent, optimal, or ideal

When someone says "It's viable," they're essentially saying: "This can hold up in the real world." It clears the bar of practicality. Whether it clears the bar of excellence is a separate question.
A Simple Test to Know When to Use "Viable"

Whenever you're unsure whether to use "viable," ask yourself: "Am I talking about whether something can realistically work, survive, or succeed in the real world?"

If yes — "viable" fits perfectly.

If you're just talking about permission ("Is it allowed?"), or raw logical possibility ("Is it conceivable?"), then "viable" is probably the wrong word. Use "allowed," "legal," "possible," or "conceivable" instead.

Viable means genuinely capable of working, surviving, or succeeding in practice — it goes beyond mere possibility to affirm that something has a solid, real-world foundation to actually function and hold together.

A viaduct is a long, elevated, bridge-like structure made up of a row of arches or spans, each one supported by tall columns or pillars, built to carry a road or railway across a valley, a stretch of low ground, or uneven terrain.

Think of it this way: imagine a row of tall stone or concrete legs, standing in a valley side by side. Now imagine a road or rail track running along the top of all those legs, high up in the air, connecting one side of the valley to the other. That is a viaduct.

A viaduct has three defining visual features:

  1. It is long. A viaduct is not a short crossing. It stretches across a considerable distance, sometimes hundreds of metres, sometimes several kilometres.
  2. It is high. It stands well above the ground, often towering over the landscape below.
  3. It has many repeated supports. Unlike a simple bridge that might be held up at just two ends, a viaduct has many equally spaced columns or piers running along its length, giving it a rhythmic, repeating appearance — like a row of teeth, or a long colonnade.

Historically, viaducts were built with stone or brick arches, which gave them a grand, almost Roman appearance. Modern viaducts are built with concrete or steel and look more industrial and sleek, but the principle is exactly the same.

A viaduct carries either:

  • A road (for cars and vehicles), or
  • A railway (for trains)

Some older or more specialised viaducts carry canals — but this is rare. The vast majority carry roads or train tracks.
Where It Is Built and Why

A viaduct is built specifically to solve a terrain problem. When engineers need to build a road or railway through a region with valleys, gorges, or low-lying ground, they have a choice: they could go the long way around, following the contours of the land (which wastes time and distance), or they could build a viaduct to maintain a straight, level path across the difficult terrain.

A viaduct, in other words, keeps the road or railway at a consistent, flat height even when the ground beneath drops sharply away. It is a feat of engineering designed to make travel efficient and direct across challenging landscapes.
How a Viaduct Differs from an Ordinary Bridge

This is the most important distinction to understand, because the two structures look and function similarly.

A bridge is typically built to cross a body of water — a river, a lake, an estuary. Its purpose is to get you from one bank to the other.

A viaduct is built primarily to cross land — a valley, a gorge, a dip in the terrain. Its purpose is to keep you elevated above uneven or low-lying ground for an extended distance.

The other key difference is length and structure. A bridge can be a single, relatively short span. A viaduct is always long, and always consists of multiple repeating spans or arches — it is essentially a chain of small bridges sitting end-to-end.

That said, in the real world, the boundary can blur. Some structures cross both land and water and are still called viaducts. The reliable rule of thumb is this: if it is long, has many repeated supporting columns, and is designed to carry a road or railway above a valley or low ground, it is a viaduct.

• The Millau Viaduct, France — One of the tallest structures in the world. It carries a motorway across the valley of the River Tarn, soaring above the clouds. Its tallest mast reaches over 340 metres.
  • The Glenfinnan Viaduct, Scotland — A curved stone railway viaduct built in the Scottish Highlands. You may recognise it from the Harry Potter films, where the Hogwarts Express crosses it.
  • The Landwasser Viaduct, Switzerland — A stunning curved railway viaduct in the Alps, known for its elegant stone arches and dramatic alpine setting.
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: a viaduct is a long, elevated, multi-arched structure that carries a road or railway over a valley or low terrain by standing on a row of tall columns.
